notes.text: Gujarati dropped the neutral vowel sound at word ends. Where Hindi says nam, Gujarati says naam and stops there.
Kem cho literally asks how are you, but kem alone means why. Tone and company decide which one you mean.
Saying tame instead of tu is not formality alone. It also softens the verb: tame aavo, not tu aav.
Grandparents split by side. Your father's parents are dada and dadi, your mother's are nana and nani.
Gujarati cooking sweetens the savoury. A pinch of gor, jaggery, goes into dal that the rest of India keeps sour.
Every number to hundred has its own shape. Ognis for nineteen looks nothing like nav, nine, or vees, twenty.
Lal means red, but for a person it means dear one. Mothers call a small child lal without thinking of colour.
Ask for the rasto, not the road. And in Gujarat a pol is a whole walled lane of houses, not a pole.
Kale means both yesterday and tomorrow. The verb tense carries the direction, so listen to the ending, not the word.
Traders built this language. Nafo means profit, khot means loss, and both turn up in ordinary kitchen conversation.
People rarely say I am ill. They say tabiyat sari nathi, the health is not good, keeping the body at a polite distance.
Ghar is the house, but ota is the raised front step where neighbours sit. Half of home life happens there.
Dhandho means trade or business, never mere labour. Asking someone's dhandho asks what they built, not who employs them.
Maja is joy, ease and pleasure at once. Maja aavi, joy came, is how you say I enjoyed that.
The Gujarati new year falls the day after Diwali, so Sal Mubarak greets a calendar the rest of India does not keep.
